Let’s dive into Chapter 10: The Challenge of Large-Scale Organization.
When an organization grows, it’s easy to get excited about all the new possibilities—efficiency, power, a bigger reach. But with that growth comes a hidden cost: complexity. And with complexity, there’s a whole new set of challenges most people don’t see coming.
Have you ever found yourself tangled up in red tape, wondering why everything suddenly feels so complicated? Maybe you’re in a big company now, spending hours filling out forms, sitting through endless meetings, and feeling like your real work is slipping through the cracks. Decisions are made by people you’ve never even met, and you can’t help but miss the days when you talked directly to your boss—when your ideas actually got noticed, and your efforts made a difference.
That’s the tricky part about large organizations. Somewhere along the way, they start seeing people as parts of a process, not as individuals. Rules and procedures take over, relationships fade into the background, and suddenly innovation gets stuck waiting for approval after approval. It’s no wonder people start to feel like what they do doesn’t really matter.
Now, think about a small nonprofit that’s trying to grow. The founders are thrilled to see their impact expand, but growth brings new problems. More resources, sure—but also more distance from their original vision. They worry: should they stay small and focused, or scale up and risk losing the very heart of what made them special?
So, what’s the answer? Is bigger always better? Turns out, that’s not really the case. Small organizations are usually more nimble, more responsive, and they hold onto that sense of community. They can pivot quickly and keep people engaged in a way that’s tough for larger organizations to match.
Here’s something important to remember: structure matters. The way you design an organization shapes everything. If you build systems that put people first—by encouraging participation, transparency, and accountability—you can actually capture the strengths of both worlds. You get the reach and resources of a large organization, without losing the flexibility and human touch of something smaller.
So, what’s the big takeaway here? The real challenge is making sure our organizations grow in ways that serve people, not the other way around. When we get that balance right, size doesn’t have to mean losing our soul.
